extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and elementary school mathematics teachers
extracted.subtask_short: notion of proof in elementary math
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and criteria for when a student's argument can count as a mathematical proof in elementary (primary) school settings, illustrated with a third-grade classroom episode. Focuses on four features of arguments plus two guiding principles for conceptualizing proof in school mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four major features determining proof
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument's status as a proof at the elementary school level is determined by the characteristics of four major features: foundation, formulation, representation, and social dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper examines these four features in an episode from a third-grade class and uses them to judge the extent to which a particular student argument could count as proof. The framework treats these four elements collectively as the basis for assessing arguments in school mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundation (one of the four major features of any given argument) — the underlying grounds or basis of the argument that support its claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the argument rests on appropriate mathematical grounds or evidence for the grade level; in the paper this feature is examined in the context of a third-grade classroom episode to evaluate whether the argument's foundations are adequate for being considered a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulation (one of the four major features of any given argument) — the way the argument is structured and expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity, logical sequencing, and the articulation of reasoning appropriate to elementary students; the paper inspects the formulation of a student's argument to determine its sufficiency as proof at that level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation (one of the four major features of any given argument) — the use of visual, symbolic, verbal, or other modes to convey the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether representations used (drawings, manipulatives, symbols, language) communicate and substantiate the reasoning in ways accessible to elementary learners; representations are analyzed in the classroom episode to see if they support treating the argument as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Social dimension (one of the four major features of any given argument) — the interpersonal and communal aspects that affect acceptance and validation of the argument as proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider classroom interaction, justification to peers/teacher, and sociomathematical norms that contribute to whether an argument is recognized as a proof; the study examines how social processes in the third-grade episode influence the argument's status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual-honesty principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellectual-honesty principle: the notion of proof in school mathematics should be conceptualized so that it is, at once, honest to mathematics as a discipline and honoring of students as mathematical learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle as a normative guide when judging whether school-level arguments count as proofs — balance fidelity to mathematical standards with respect for students' developmental levels and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuum principle: there should be continuity in how the notion of proof is conceptualized in different grade levels so that students’ experiences with proof in school have coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this principle to ensure that expectations and conceptualizations of proof are coherent across grades, supporting progressive development of students' proving practices rather than abrupt shifts in standards.
